items.fromString:
RHBK 26.6.2 introduced a breaking change: the introspection endpoint now returns active: false if the authenticated client is not in the token's aud claim.

Issued tokens have aud: "account" and azp: <client_id>. Zync creates OIDC clients without an audience mapper, so the application client is never added to aud. RHBK 26.6.2+ rejects introspection with:

  error="invalid_token", reason="Client '<client_id>' is not in the token audience"

Workaround:

  Add to RHBK CR:

   spec:
     additionalOptions:
       - name: spi-login-protocol--openid-connect--allow-token-introspection-without-audience-check
          value: "true"

Permanent fix:

   Application's client_id must be included in the token's aud claim. This can be achieved by Zync adding an audience mapper when creating OIDC clients in RHBK.

## Operator Instructions — Database Encryption

Zync now encrypts sensitive database fields (tenant access tokens) at rest. Two new **mandatory** environment variables must be provided to every Zync deployment (both `zync-puma` and `zync-que`):

| Variable | Purpose | Format |
|----------|---------|--------|
| `ZYNC_DATABASE_ENCRYPT_KEY` | Primary encryption key | Random string, min 12 characters (recommended: 32 alphanumeric) |
| `ZYNC_DATABASE_ENCRYPT_SALT` | Key derivation salt | Random string, min 20 characters (recommended: 32 alphanumeric) |

### Generating values

Use any cryptographically secure random generator. Examples:

```
# Option A: openssl
openssl rand -base64 32 | tr -d '/+=' | head -c 32

# Option B: Ruby
ruby -e "require 'securerandom'; puts SecureRandom.alphanumeric(32)"
```

Generate **one key and one salt per environment** (e.g., one pair for staging, a different pair for production). Both values must be identical across all Zync pods in the same environment.

### Deployment

- Both variables are **required** — Zync will fail to encrypt/decrypt tokens without them.
- Existing data (plaintext tokens) will continue to work. New and updated tokens are encrypted automatically.
- No data migration is needed at deploy time.

### Encrypting all existing tokens

There are two ways to encrypt all existing plaintext tokens after deployment:

1. **From Zync** (re-encrypts in place): `Tenant.find_each(&:encrypt)` in a Rails console.
2. **From Porta** (full resync): `rails zync:resync:full` — this pushes all access tokens from Porta to Zync, where they get encrypted with the current primary key on write. This is also useful as a recovery mechanism if the encryption key is lost (see below).

### Key rotation

If a key is compromised, `ZYNC_DATABASE_ENCRYPT_KEY` accepts **comma-separated keys** for rotation:

1. Generate a new key.
2. Set the variable to `<old-key>,<new-key>` (old first, new last).
3. Deploy. Zync will decrypt with both keys, encrypt new data with the new key.
4. Re-encrypt existing rows: run `Tenant.find_each(&:encrypt)` in a Zync Rails console.
5. Verify all rows are encrypted: `Tenant.find_each { |t| puts "#{t.id} unencrypted" unless t.encrypted_attribute?(:access_token) }`
6. Once all rows are re-encrypted, remove the old key — set the variable to just `<new-key>`.

The **last key** in the comma-separated list is always used for new encryptions. All keys are tried for decryption.

### Recovery if the primary key is lost

If the encryption key is lost and encrypted tokens can no longer be decrypted:

1. Generate a new key and salt, and configure them in Zync.
2. Run `rails zync:resync:full` from **Porta** — this re-sends all access tokens from Porta to Zync, where they will be encrypted with the new key.

This works because Porta is the source of truth for access tokens. The resync overwrites all tokens in Zync's database with freshly encrypted values.

### Rollback warning

If Zync is rolled back to a version without encryption support, the app will read raw ciphertext (JSON blobs) from the database instead of decrypted tokens. This won't crash but will silently break API calls to Porta. Before rolling back, ensure either:

- No tokens have been encrypted yet (fresh deployment), or
- The database is restored to a pre-encryption backup, or
- After rollback, run `rails zync:resync:full` from Porta to overwrite encrypted values with plaintext.

### What NOT to do

- **Do not lose the key without a recovery plan.** There is no built-in recovery mechanism — but a full resync from Porta (`rails zync:resync:full`) can restore all tokens. Treat the key like a database password: back it up securely.
- **Do not reuse keys across environments.** Each environment should have its own unique key and salt.
- **Do not change the salt during rotation.** Only the key rotates; the salt stays the same for the lifetime of the environment. Changing the salt breaks decryption of all existing encrypted data.

### Reference

See the [Rails Active Record Encryption guide](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/v8.0/active_record_encryption.html) for full details on the encryption framework.

items.fromString: When Zync attempts a request to Porta's API with a recently-rotated token, the request may fail with a 401 if the token was replaced between the time Zync received it and the time it used it. Zync should implement retry logic for authentication errors: on a 401, it should request a fresh token from Porta (via the tenant endpoint) and retry the failed request. This handles the race condition window during token rotation gracefully, without requiring longer token validity periods.
items.toString:
After [https://github.com/3scale/porta/pull/4310|https://github.com/3scale/porta/pull/4310|smart-link] , Zync is going to receive tokens that will expire a day after being received. Zync doesn’t have the capacity to request new tokens, it just gets the tokens from porta when it receives a notification. One possible but unlikely scenario is when the last notification was received more than a day ago but the update job in zync queue still haven’t been processed. In that case, the job will be lost.

This issue is about adding a retry logic so the job has a few more hours to wait for a new token before being definitely discarded.

As 3scale approaches End of Life (EOL), we want to ensure that users retain the capability to continue operating or upgrading their environments with newer component versions without being restricted by  validation limits. Responsibility for running unsupported configurations will be explicitly shifted to the user.
Currently, {{maxOCPVersion}} in the 3scale in the operator bundle metadata installation and upgrade workflows enforce strict validation of OpenShift versions.  If using newer untested OCP versions, the process is blocked.

The goal of this task is to modify *any checks so that they no longer block installation or upgrade* when newer, unsupported, or not yet tested component versions are detected. Instead of failing the process, the system should allow it to continue while clearly displaying warnings to the user.

In parallel to this task, we need to ensure also that pre-flight checks only enforce _lower_ version limits. Customers should be able to use newer database versions than the ones officially supported, with the operator not blocking upper limits.

items.fromString:
h2. Problem

The async Redis client in {{lib/3scale/backend/storage_async/client.rb}} leaks connections under concurrent load when Redis connection errors trigger the retry logic.

The upstream {{async-redis}} gem (v0.13.1) correctly caches sentinel clients in {{SentinelClient}}, so sentinel connections themselves are not leaked. However, our {{StorageAsync::Client}} wrapper has a race condition in its {{with_reconnect}} method that creates and leaks entire {{SentinelClient}} instances (each owning a connection pool and sentinel connections).

h2. Root Cause: Race Condition in {{with_reconnect}}

{{StorageAsync::Client}} is a singleton shared by all fibers. The {{with_reconnect}} method wraps every Redis operation:

{code:ruby}def with_reconnect
  attempt = 0
  begin
    yield connect          # connect does: @redis_async ||= AsyncRedis::Client.connect(@opts)
  rescue *CONNECTION_ERRORS => e
    close                  # close does: @redis_async&.close; @redis_async = nil
    # ... attempt tracking, sleep, retry
  end
end{code}

In async mode, multiple fibers execute concurrently within the same reactor, sharing the {{@redis_async}} instance variable. When the Redis master goes down, many fibers fail simultaneously and enter the rescue block. Since fibers yield cooperatively at I/O points, the interleaving is:

# *Fiber A* catches {{CONNECTION_ERROR}}, calls {{close}} → calls {{@redis_async.close}} (I/O — *yields here*).
# *Fiber B* resumes, also catches {{CONNECTION_ERROR}}, calls {{close}} → {{@redis_async}} is still the same object (fiber A hasn't set it to nil yet), so fiber B also calls {{.close}} on it.
# *Fiber A* resumes, finishes {{close}}: sets {{@redis_async = nil}}. Calls {{sleep}} → *yields*.
# *Fiber B* finishes {{close}}: sets {{@redis_async = nil}} (no-op). Calls {{sleep}} → *yields*.
# *Fiber A* wakes up, {{retry}} → {{connect}} → {{@redis_async ||=}} creates *Client #1*. The pool's constructor block calls {{resolve_master}} via sentinels. {{yield connect}} passes Client #1 to the block.
# *Fiber B* wakes up, {{retry}} → {{connect}} → {{@redis_async}} is already Client #1, reuses it. {{yield connect}} passes Client #1 to the block.
# Both fibers now execute their Redis operation. If the master is still down, both fail again.
# *Fiber A* enters rescue, calls {{close}} → closes Client #1, sets {{@redis_async = nil}}. *Yields* during close.
# *Fiber B* enters rescue, calls {{close}} → {{@redis_async}} is nil → {{nil&.close}} is a no-op. Sets {{@redis_async = nil}}.
# *Fiber A* wakes, {{retry}} → {{connect}} → creates *Client #2*.
# Meanwhile, *Fiber C* (which was executing a different Redis operation successfully) now tries a new operation → {{connect}} returns Client #2 → operation fails (master still down) → {{close}} → *destroys Client #2*.
# *Fiber A* still holds Client #2 in its local {{conn}} variable (from {{yield connect}}), but Client #2 has been closed by Fiber C.

Each cycle through this loop creates a new client. With N concurrent fibers and the worker configured with {{reconnect_attempts: Float::INFINITY}}, this creates a steady stream of leaked clients.

h2. Why Leaked Clients Are Not Garbage Collected

Each {{Async::Redis::SentinelClient}} (or {{Client}}) holds a connection pool ({{Async::Pool::Controller}}). When the pool creates its first resource, it spawns a gardener task via {{Async(transient: true)}}. This gardener task is a child of the reactor and holds a closure over the pool controller ({{self.close}} in the ensure block). The reference chain is:

*Reactor → gardener task → closure → pool controller → TCP connections*

Even after {{@redis_async}} no longer references a leaked client, the reactor still holds its gardener task, which keeps the pool and all its connections alive. The GC cannot collect any of it. Connections accumulate indefinitely.

h2. Impact

In production, this manifests as unbounded connection growth on Redis sentinels and master. A customer reported connections growing from 225 to 1194+ on a single sentinel ([THREESCALE-14671|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/THREESCALE-14671]). The problem only occurs with async Redis + sentinels, because the sentinel architecture amplifies the leak: each leaked client creates connections to all sentinels (to resolve the master) plus connections to the master itself.

h2. Previous Work

A related leak was fixed on the 2.x branch in [THREESCALE-14671|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/THREESCALE-14671] / [PR #467|https://github.com/3scale/apisonator/pull/467]. That fix addressed a different variant of the problem specific to the custom {{SentinelsClientACLTLS}} class used on 2.x. On master, the upstream {{SentinelClient}} handles sentinel caching correctly, but the {{with_reconnect}} race condition described above remains.

h2. Fix

Remove the {{close}} call from {{with_reconnect}}. Instead of destroying and recreating the entire client on connection errors, just sleep and retry.

The underlying connection pool ({{Async::Pool::Controller}}) already handles dead connections correctly: when a connection fails, the pool retires it (removes it from the pool and closes it) and creates a new one via its constructor block, which re-resolves the master address through sentinels. The pool is designed for exactly this scenario.

By not destroying the client, we avoid the race condition entirely — there is only ever one client instance, and the pool manages individual connections within it.
